cues.text: A Boy Martyr
Pancras (Pancratius) is remembered by ancient tradition as a mere teenager, with some accounts saying he was only fourteen years old.
He was martyred for the Christian faith, most probably, according to the Catholic Encyclopedia, either during the persecution of Valerian in the 250s or that of Diocletian around 304.
His extreme youth at the time of his death made him, from an early date, one of the Roman Church's most affecting examples of martyrdom.
Burial on the Via Aurelia
Pancras was buried in a catacomb along the Via Aurelia , distinct from the resting place of Nereus and Achilleus on the Via Ardeatina.
The Church came to commemorate all of these Roman martyrs together on the same day, 12 May.
A church was erected over his grave around the turn of the sixth century, a building that, in altered form, still stands on the site today.
Widespread and Enduring Devotion
Devotion to Pancras spread with unusual speed beyond Rome itself.
Later tradition associates relics of the young martyr with the Gregorian mission to England, though the surviving evidence for their transfer is uncertain.
An early church at Canterbury was dedicated in his honor — a dedication that gave his name, centuries later, to the London district and railway station of St Pancras.
A Name Invoked Against False Oaths
Popular devotion in the Middle Ages came to invoke Pancras particularly as a swift avenger of perjury.
This tradition reflected the ancient practice of swearing solemn oaths upon relics of the saints.
Folk belief held that those who lied while invoking his name would meet with sudden and unpleasant consequences.
Legacy
As with many of the earliest Roman martyrs, few reliable historical details survive beyond his burial place and the fact of his martyrdom.
Pancras remains venerated to this day as one of the youngest named martyrs of the early Church.
His memory is carried by his ancient Roman church, his English dedication at Canterbury, and the wider devotion that grew from Pope Gregory's missionary relics.
